strengths: The paper targets a real bottleneck in joint text-speech spoken language modeling: the length and alignment mismatch between text tokens and speech tokens. The idea of explicitly text-aligning speech-side representations is conceptually clean and relevant.

The proposed system is technically plausible and combines existing components into a coherent pipeline: frozen Whisper encoder, cross-attention aggregation, RVQ quantization, reconstruction via speech units/vocoder, and LoRA-based SLM training.

The manuscript includes several evaluation angles, including reconstruction metrics, human listening tests, continuation evaluation, likelihood-based benchmarks, spoken QA, robustness to noise, ASR ablations, and module ablations.
The low-frequency aligned token representation and the speech-editing examples suggest that the method may capture some paralinguistic information in a controllable way.
weaknesses: The central low-bitrate claim is substantially confounded. TASTE relies on text transcriptions during tokenization and decoding, but the bitrate accounting appears to exclude the text side channel that carries most lexical/semantic information. This makes comparisons to speech-only codecs/tokenizers misleading.

The reconstruction evaluation overstates the evidence. The text-only baseline is already very strong on UTMOS/DNSMOS and TASTE mainly improves selected metrics such as WER, duration, and MUSHRA; it is not clear that the speech tokens themselves carry broad paralinguistic information beyond what the text-conditioned decoder, speaker embedding, and S3/vocoder stack already provide.

The spoken language modeling comparisons are not clean. Baselines differ in base model, scale, training data, decoding strategy, and whether they are cascaded or end-to-end. The strongest gains seem concentrated in text-heavy metrics such as StoryCloze and GPT-4o-on-ASR-transcripts, while acoustic likelihood results are mixed or worse than some prior models.

The evaluation protocol is weak for the paper's claims. GPT-4o semantic MOS on ASR transcripts mostly evaluates text continuation, not spoken language modeling quality; human evaluation uses only 20 samples per method with very large standard deviations; significance testing and more rigorous subjective evaluation are missing.

Novelty is limited by the reliance on straightforward combinations of known mechanisms: ASR-conditioned cross-attention, RVQ, reconstruction training, S3 unit targets, and LoRA adaptation. The claimed end-to-end/tokenization novelty is weakened by the dependence on external ASR, frozen encoders, pretrained vocoders, and word-level averaging/replication to handle tokenizer mismatch.

The one-to-one alignment story is less clean than advertised. Appendix A.4 shows that ASR-token and LLM-token vocabularies require word-level grouping, averaging, and expansion, which reintroduces heuristic alignment machinery and undermines the claim of straightforward alignment.

Important reproducibility details are missing or incomplete: the abstract leaves the code/demo/model URL blank; exact model variants, SLM training duration/steps, decoding/sampling settings, data filtering, ASR settings, and evaluation implementation details are insufficient for reliable reproduction.

The ethical discussion identifies voice imitation and speech editing risks but offers only generic mitigations. Given the explicit voice manipulation capability and proposed release of models/demo, stronger safeguards, consent assumptions, watermarking/provenance plans, and misuse analysis are needed.

Overall, the paper is understandable and technically plausible, but the main claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The confounded comparisons and insufficiently controlled evaluation are major issues for a top-tier AI venue.

Several claims are overstated. The work is described as end-to-end and as a speech tokenizer, but it depends on ASR text and multiple pretrained components, and the method is closer to transcript-conditioned paralinguistic/prosody tokenization than a general speech tokenizer.

Evaluation quality is weak for a top-tier claim: human tests use only 20 samples per method with large variance, GPT-4o scoring is based on ASR transcripts and may miss audio failures, and no convincing significance analysis or broad-domain listening evaluation is provided.
